Research problem: In MVFA's few-shot setting, can the K labelled abnormal support images with pixel masks be dropped entirely, adapting the residual adapters per target modality from the K normal support images alone with synthesised lesions (patch pasting and intensity-perturbed blobs whose synthetic masks supervise the Dice + Focal losses), and how much of the image- and pixel-level AUROC of the standard K-normal + K-masked-abnormal protocol does this normal-only variant retain for K in {2, 4, 8, 16}?
Rationale: The released code defines 'K-shot' as K normal plus K abnormal images with masks from BMAD's valid split (G4), so the paper's few-shot numbers assume the expensive part of clinical labelling, while a clinic adopting a new modality usually has only normal studies at hand; the segmentation branch has no other supervision route (G3). None of these measures what MVFA's multi-level adapters lose when the abnormal support set is removed. The problem changes one input of one stage (the support set of the few-shot fine-tuning), needs only the public code and BMAD, and has a direct measurable outcome: the fraction of K+K performance retained per modality and K, with 3 support draws under the shared protocol.

Target paper title: Adapting Visual-Language Models for Generalizable Anomaly Detection in Medical Images
Target paper abstract: Recent advancements in large-scale visual-language pre-trained models have led to significant progress in zero-/few-shot anomaly detection within natural image domains. However, the substantial domain divergence between natural and medical images limits the effectiveness of these methodologies in medical anomaly detection. This paper introduces a novel lightweight multi-level adaptation and comparison framework to repurpose the CLIP model for medical anomaly detection. Our approach integrates multiple residual adapters into the pre-trained visual encoder, enabling a stepwise enhancement of visual features across different levels. This multi-level adaptation is guided by multi-level, pixel-wise visual-language feature alignment loss functions, which recalibrate the model's focus from object semantics in natural imagery to anomaly identification in medical images. The adapted features exhibit improved generalization across various medical data types, even in zero-shot scenarios where the model encounters unseen medical modalities and anatomical regions during training. Our experiments on medical anomaly detection benchmarks demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art models, with an average AUC improvement of 6.24% and 7.33% for anomaly classification, 2.03% and 2.37% for anomaly segmentation, under the zero-shot and few-shot settings, respectively. Source code is available at: https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/MVFA-AD
Limitations to address:

The detection (classification) adapters receive an image-level BCE loss on every source image, including the three BMAD datasets that have no masks (OCT17, ChestXray, HIS). The segmentation adapters, which produce the anomaly maps, are trained only with Dice and Focal losses on pixel-level masks, i.e. only on BrainMRI, LiverCT and RESC. Localisation therefore depends entirely on dense expert masks from three datasets; no image-level, sparse or normal-only supervision of the segmentation branch is formulated.
- G4. The few-shot setting needs labelled abnormal images with masks and is evaluated on one draw: In the released code, 'K-shot' means K normal AND K abnormal images, the abnormal ones with pixel masks, both drawn from BMAD's valid/ split; the adapters are fine-tuned on them per target task. Clinical few-shot supervision may instead contain only normal or unlabelled images, which the method does not support. Only one fixed draw per dataset is provided. Training time and compute for the per-task fine-tuning are not reported.

Problem: When MVFA's few-shot adaptation receives only K normal support images (no abnormal images, no masks), should synthesised lesions supervise only the segmentation adapters, only the detection adapters, or both, and how much of the image- and pixel-level AUROC of the standard K-normal + K-masked-abnormal protocol does the best normal-only variant retain for K in {2, 4, 8, 16} over three support draws?

Rationale: The released code defines 'K-shot' as K normal plus K abnormal images with masks (G4), so MVFA's few-shot numbers assume the expensive part of clinical labelling, and the segmentation branch has no other route to supervision (G3). MediCLIP [10] and SpatioPrompt [20] show that CLIP can be adapted from normal images with anomaly synthesis, but in single-branch designs; MVFA separates detection and segmentation adapters at four levels, and synthetic lesions are known to transfer imperfectly to real pathology, so which branch should consume synthetic supervision is an open design question specific to the target method. Synthesis follows MediCLIP's published recipe (fixed families and parameters), so the only variable is where the synthetic supervision is applied. The outcome answers a practical question, whether a clinic needs any annotated abnormal studies to adapt MVFA, and the three-draw protocol also answers the single-draw part of G4. Few-shot fine-tuning takes minutes per run on one GPU.
